lines: Let's start with what goes in a spec. The textbook line, which the tool makers repeated, is that a spec says what to build. How to build it goes in a separate design or plan document.

And users don't do that. In the repo sample, seventy-seven point six percent of specs contain implementation detail, and in fifty-eight percent it takes up a section or more. Of those, three quarters name specific classes, functions, file paths, data structures, or library versions.

Two reasons from the interviews. First, they add detail when they don't trust the agent with a hard task. One team specifies the how only where they believe the AI has very low capability. Second, they add knowledge the agent can't infer. Internal APIs, error codes, domain rules, team conventions.

They are. But there's a cost no participant mentioned. Class names and library versions change every time you refactor, while the intended behavior stays the same. So a spec loaded with implementation detail goes stale faster.
[thoughtful] So the detail that helps the agent today is the detail that rots the spec later.

That's the tension. The second finding is that SDD is used selectively, mostly by task size. Big features get a spec. Bugs, hotfixes, scripts, and prototypes get a direct prompt. An estimated eighty-two percent of specs in the sample describe new features. Only about sixteen percent involve fixes.
Which sounds sensible until you look at the gap.

Exactly. Small changes get no spec, but a small change can touch ten other features. A production hotfix changes behavior with no written intent at all. And nobody described a team-level rule for what warrants a spec. Every developer sets their own threshold.
